In Gram staining, gram-negative cells appear pink because they lose the crystal violet-iodine complex during the decolourisation step. This is due to their thin peptidoglycan layer and outer membrane. After decolourisation, the counterstain, safranin, is applied. Safranin stains the gram-negative cells pink or red, making them visible under the microscope. In contrast, gram-positive cells retain the purple color from the crystal violet-iodine complex.

If the demand for rice is elastic, it means that when the price of rice goes up, people buy much less rice. In the example, a 10% price increase led to a 25% drop in how much rice people wanted to buy. This big drop in demand means that the total money made from selling rice decreases when prices go up. So, elastic demand shows that people are sensitive to price changes and will buy significantly less if prices rise.

Cassava must be processed before consumption to reduce the risk of cyanide poisoning. The roots contain cyanogenic glucosides, mainly linamarin, which release hydrogen cyanide when damaged. Processing methods like fermentation, grating, roasting, and sun-drying break cells, activate enzymes, and remove cyanide, lowering the cyanide content to safe levels. Without proper processing, cassava can cause konzo, a paralytic disease, especially in communities relying on it during food shortages.

Cassava roots contain cyanogenic glucosides, mainly linamarin, which release hydrogen cyanide when damaged. Processing reduces this hazard. To make garri, peeled roots are grated, packed into sacks, and left to ferment for two to four days while water is pressed out; the mash is sieved and roasted. Grating breaks the cells so that the enzyme linamarase can act on linamarin, and roasting drives off much of the remaining hydrogen cyanide. Sun-drying thin chips also lowers cyanide content, but more slowly. For this course, a total cyanide content of 10 mg per kg in the finished flour is the reference safety limit. Poorly processed cassava has been linked to konzo, a paralytic disease, in communities that depend heavily on cassava during food shortages.
